catalog_quote: The accent is a quality of vowels and consists of a pitch, higher than that of the other vowel(s) of the same word, usually combined with a higher degree of loudness (stress). As this higher degree of loudness is not always heard, it apparently is less essential than the high pitch is, but the stress is observable in the majority of cases and therefore it must be mentioned here. ... Most words have one and only one accent; exceptions to this rule will be discussed separately below. ... So in a word there usually is one vowel, and that always the same, which has the accent. However, there is no rule by which the place of the accent in all words is determined. ... 1° distinctive value for words. This only applies to plurivocalic words, because in these the place of the accent is as distinctive as the character and order of the constituent phonemes are. This distinctive value is, once more…

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation and locator check out verbatim in the Anceaux 1965 text we hold (pp. 36-39, 62-63). (2) The classification rests on the standard reference grammar, which has a dedicated accent chapter with minimal pairs by accent place and an explicit 'no rule' statement; it is Glottolog's top description and no instrumental or later published phonology supersedes it. (3) The one later first-hand phonology, May & May 1981, was downloaded now (stress section complete): one stress per phonological word, ultimate or penultimate mostly with a few antepenultimate, morphologically conditioned in verbs, a tendency for stress on a closed syllable in non-verbal words 'although there are exceptions', otherwise 'no general rule governs stress placement. sources.quote: p. 10: 'A phonological word (PW) is defined as a phonological unit having one stressed syllable (Ś). There may be a pre-margin of a number of unstressed syllables (Sn) and a post-margin of up to two unstressed syllables (S)... PW = (Sn) Ś (S) (S). Stress placement patterns are of two main types, ultimate and penultimate stress. A relatively small number of words have antepenultimate stress. In verbal forms stress placement is morphologically conditioned (Anceaux pp. 38, 62ff). In non-verbal forms the stress usually falls on a closed syllable where one occurs, although there are exceptions. W
